query: For high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles intended for catalysis, sensing, energy storage, corrosion-related uses, and other applications requiring thermal stability, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs their premelting and melting behavior and why? Specify a controlled comparison that would reveal the governing factor, the observations expected relative to a baseline, the range over which the hypothesis should hold, prior evidence that supports it, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: The premelting and melting behavior of high‐entropy alloy nanoparticles is primarily governed by their intrinsic atomic‐scale chemical heterogeneity. In these nanoparticles, the compositional disorder induces localized lattice strain, short‐range chemical clustering, and/or surface segregation of lower melting point elements. These features create regions with reduced cohesive energy that act as nucleation sites for premelting, thereby lowering the effective melting onset compared to nanoparticles with more chemically uniform structures.
generation.material_initial_state: Single-phase high-entropy alloy nanoparticles containing five or more principal elements that are synthesized to yield an overall uniform composition yet retain inherent atomic-scale inhomogeneities (e.g., localized lattice distortions and minor deviations in surface composition).
generation.intervention: Perform controlled heating experiments comparing nanoparticles engineered to promote atomic-scale chemical heterogeneity (via treatments that induce short-range ordering or surface segregation) against a baseline group of nanoparticles with enhanced chemical homogeneity, or conventional monometallic/binary nanoparticles of similar size and morphology.
generation.conditions: Experiments conducted under inert (e.g., argon) or vacuum conditions with identical thermal ramping protocols from room temperature up to near the bulk melting point. Nanoparticle size, shape, and support should be maintained constant to isolate the effects of compositional heterogeneity.
generation.structural_mediator: Localized lattice distortions, defect sites, and surface regions exhibiting non-uniform bonding due to compositional fluctuations.
generation.mechanism: Multiple principal elements in the alloy lead to variations in local bond strengths and lattice strains. These inhomogeneities—whether as internal short-range order or as surface segregation of lower melting constituents—reduce the local cohesive energy, making it easier for atoms at these sites to become mobile at lower temperatures. This early surface disordering (premelting) then accelerates the overall melting process.
generation.predicted_outcome: Nanoparticles with enhanced atomic-scale heterogeneity (or induced surface segregation) will demonstrate an earlier onset of surface disordering and a depressed overall melting temperature relative to those with homogeneous chemical distributions or to comparable monometallic/binary nanoparticles.
generation.baseline: Chemically homogeneous nanoparticles, including monometallic or binary nanoparticles of comparable size, shape, and support.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is expected to apply to nanoparticles typically below ~100 nm in diameter and which possess a high configurational entropy; its validity in bulk materials or in systems with very low atomic size mismatch may be limited.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative contribution of internal lattice strain versus surface segregation to the melting behavior is not fully resolved, and variations in synthesis or particle size might influence the magnitude of the melting point depression.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two sets of high-entropy alloy nanoparticles with identical overall compositions and sizes. In one set, employ post-synthesis thermal or chemical treatments to deliberately enhance atomic-scale chemical heterogeneity (e.g., promoting short-range ordering or surface segregation). In the control set, optimize the synthesis to yield a more chemically homogeneous distribution. Subject both sets to identical controlled heating under an inert atmosphere while monitoring structural evolution using in situ TEM and differential scanning calorimetry (DSC). Complement these observations with surface compositional analysis (such as atom probe tomography or high-resolution EDS mapping).
measurements: Onset temperature of surface disordering (premelting) via in situ TEM imaging
Thermal transition features (e.g., endothermic peaks) using DSC
Surface and local composition profiles using atom probe tomography/EDS
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the nanoparticles with enhanced chemical heterogeneity do not exhibit a statistically significant lower premelting onset temperature and overall melting point compared to the homogeneous control group (or if observed differences can be solely attributed to variations in particle size, shape, or support effects), then the hypothesis that atomic-scale chemical heterogeneity governs the premelting and melting behavior is falsified.

High-entropy alloys (HEAs), consisting of five or more principal elements with a near equimolar ratio, have become one of the most transformative concepts in current alloy design. Homogenous mixing of a large number of elements induces synergistic effects among different elements, thus resulting in an unusual combination of functional properties appealing to a broad range of applications such as structural alloys, catalysis, sensing, and energy storage. While the synthesis of bulk HEAs has been the main focus in the past decade, nano-sized HEA particles are emerging as a new class of multifunctional materials due to their more fascinating properties. Scalable and economically viable synthetic methods for HEA nanoparticles (NPs) are of particular interest, yet the controlled incorporation of multiple elements into a tiny particle (<100 nm) remains a significant challenge. A wide range of researches have revealed that the nanoparticles loading on the supports could significantly improve specific surface area and surface energy compared with the bulk materials or the nanoparticles themselves,. AbstractDirect formation of ultra-small nanoparticles on carbon supports by rapid high temperature synthesis method offers new opportunities for scalable nanomanufacturing and the synthesis of stable multi-elemental nanoparticles. However, the underlying mechanisms affecting the dispersion and stability of nanoparticles on the supports during high temperature processing remain enigmatic. In this work, we report the observation of metallic nanoparticles formation and stabilization on carbon supports through in situ Joule heating method. We find that the formation of metallic nanoparticles is associated with the simultaneous phase transition of amorphous carbon to a highly defective turbostratic graphite (T-graphite). Molecular dynamic (MD) simulations suggest that the defective T-graphite provide numerous nucleation sites for the nanoparticles to form. drafts.hypothesis: For high‐entropy‐alloy (HEA) nanoparticles, the nature and degree of atomic-scale chemical heterogeneity—specifically, the presence of short-range order or local elemental segregation versus homogeneous mixing—governs the initiation of premelting and the overall melting behavior.
drafts.material_initial_state: Nanoparticles of HEAs synthesized to have identical overall compositions but differing in their atomic-scale mixing: one set with near‐ideal homogeneous alloying and another set engineered to display controlled short-range chemical order or local elemental clustering.
drafts.intervention: Prepare two sets of HEA nanoparticles with identical bulk compositions and particle sizes (e.g., 10–50 nm) where one set is processed to achieve maximum atomic-level mixing (minimal chemical heterogeneity) and the other is thermally or chemically treated to induce controlled short-range segregation.
drafts.conditions: The experiments should be conducted under identical thermal ramping conditions (e.g., using in situ heating in a TEM or DSC measurements) in an inert atmosphere to avoid oxidation, over a temperature range covering the expected premelting onset to complete melting.
drafts.structural_mediator: Atomic-level chemical heterogeneity that modulates local cohesive energies and surface energy distributions.
drafts.mechanism: Homogeneously mixed HEA nanoparticles display uniformly high local activation energies for atomic rearrangement, delaying the onset of surface atom mobility that leads to premelting. In contrast, localized regions of elemental segregation reduce local bonding strengths, thereby creating sites that act as nucleation points for premelting, which lowers the effective premelting and melting temperatures.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Under identical heating conditions, nanoparticles with induced short-range order (or local segregation) will exhibit a statistically significant lower onset temperature for premelting (and a slightly reduced overall melting point) compared to their homogenously mixed counterparts.
drafts.baseline: Nanoparticles with near-ideal atomic-level mixing, where melting behavior reflects the bulk high-entropy stabilization.
drafts.boundary: The hypothesis is expected to hold for HEA nanoparticles within the size range of approximately 10–50 nm and for compositions where high configurational entropy is a dominant factor in stabilizing the solid phase; extrapolation beyond these conditions (e.g., very large particles or bulk alloys) may introduce additional size- or strain-related effects not captured by this hypothesis.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two sets of HEA nanoparticles with identical bulk compositions and sizes. Engineer one set for maximal atomic homogeneity and induce controlled short-range order in the other set. Using in situ TEM heating and/or DSC, measure the temperature at which premelting (as evidenced by initial surface atom mobilization) and full melting occur. Compare these temperatures statistically between the two sets.
measurements: Premelting onset temperature (e.g., from TEM observations of surface disordering)
Complete melting temperature (e.g., from DSC endothermic peaks)
Characterization of atomic-level mixing via techniques such as atom-probe tomography or high-resolution EDS mapping
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If no statistically significant difference in the onset of premelting or melting temperature is observed between the nanoparticles with induced short-range order and the homogeneously mixed nanoparticles, then the hypothesis that atomic-scale chemical heterogeneity governs the premelting and melting behavior is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: In high-entropy alloy nanoparticles, the onset of premelting and melting is primarily governed by surface segregation of the lower melting point constituent elements, which creates localized regions of weakened bonding that initiate melting.
drafts.material_initial_state: High-entropy alloy nanoparticles with a nominally uniform multi-element composition.
drafts.intervention: Prepare two sets of HEA nanoparticles: one with standard synthesis yielding a relatively homogeneous surface composition (baseline) and another where post‐synthesis thermal or chemical treatments promote enhanced surface segregation of lower melting point elements.
drafts.conditions: Experiments conducted over a range of nanoparticle sizes within the studied application range (e.g., 5–50 nm) under controlled inert or vacuum atmospheres to avoid oxidation effects.
drafts.structural_mediator: Surface atomic composition and local interfacial disorder.
drafts.mechanism: Enhanced segregation of lower melting point elements at the nanoparticle surface reduces local cohesive energy, creating defects that serve as nucleation sites for premelting. This localized weakening accelerates surface melting relative to particles where the composition remains homogeneous.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Nanoparticles with induced surface segregation will exhibit a lower onset temperature for premelting and a broader melting transition compared to the baseline particles with a uniform surface composition.
drafts.baseline: HEA nanoparticles synthesized to maintain homogeneous surface and bulk compositions.
drafts.boundary: The hypothesis is expected to hold for HEAs with sufficient atomic size mismatch or elemental enthalpy differences that favor segregation, and over the nanoparticle size range where surface-to-volume effects predominate.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two sets of HEA nanoparticles: one with controlled homogeneous composition and one with a post‐synthesis thermal treatment designed to enhance surface segregation. Use differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) to measure premelting and melting onset temperatures and combine these with high-resolution surface compositional analysis (e.g., atom probe tomography or EDS in TEM) to confirm surface composition differences.
measurements: Surface composition profiles via atom probe tomography or EDS
Morphological evolution via TEM during in situ heating
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If nanoparticles with artificially enhanced surface segregation do not show a statistically significant decrease in the premelting onset temperature (or exhibit similar melting behavior) compared to the homogeneous baseline, then the hypothesis that surface segregation governs premelting and melting behavior is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: The onset of premelting and the overall melting behavior in high‐entropy alloy nanoparticles are governed by the strength of the nanoparticle–support interface. In nanoparticles that interact strongly with their support (via a high density of defects or anchoring sites that lead to enhanced interfacial binding), surface atom mobility is reduced and premelting is delayed relative to nanoparticles on inert supports.
drafts.material_initial_state: Single-phase high‐entropy alloy nanoparticles (e.g., those synthesized by rapid high‐temperature methods or electrospinning/annealing) uniformly dispersed on granular supports.
drafts.intervention: Prepare two sets of HEA nanoparticles that are identical in composition and size, then deposit one set on a support known to provide strong interfacial binding (e.g. defective turbostratic graphite or activated carbon) and the other on an inert support (e.g. SiO2 or chemically inert alumina).
drafts.conditions: Heat both samples under identical inert or controlled atmospheres (e.g., high-purity argon), using a thermal ramp from room temperature to temperatures approaching the alloy’s bulk melting point, while monitoring the melting process using techniques such as DSC/TGA and in situ TEM.
drafts.structural_mediator: The nanoparticle–support interface structure, specifically the density of defect or anchoring sites and the degree of short-range atomic ordering at the surface.
drafts.mechanism: Strong interfacial bonding reduces surface atomic mobility by increasing the activation energy required for surface diffusion and disorder. This delay in surface reordering suppresses premelting phenomena relative to particles on inert supports, where higher surface energy and fewer bonding constraints lead to an earlier onset of disorder.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Nanoparticles on high-binding (defective) supports will show a higher onset temperature for premelting (and a sharper melting transition) compared to those on inert supports. Smaller particles (with a higher surface-area-to-volume ratio) will exhibit a more pronounced difference.
drafts.baseline: Unsupported HEA nanoparticles or those on inert, low-binding-energy supports, which exhibit the conventional melting point depression and early premelting typical of nanoscale materials.
drafts.boundary: This effect is expected to be most significant for nanoparticles in the 5–100 nm size range and for HEA compositions with similar inherent configurational entropy; if the support itself chemically reacts or alloys with the nanoparticles, the mechanism may not apply.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize identical HEA nanoparticles and deposit them on two different supports: one with a high density of defect sites (e.g., defective turbostratic graphite) and one inert support (e.g., SiO2). Subject both samples to identical controlled heating (using DSC/TGA and in situ TEM or XRD) to capture the temperature at which premelting (surface disordering) and bulk melting events occur. Also systematically vary particle sizes to determine the surface-to-volume effect.
measurements: Differential Scanning Calorimetry (DSC) to detect endothermic events signaling premelting/melting
Thermogravimetric Analysis (TGA) to record changes in mass or oxidation onset
In situ TEM or XRD to directly observe the structural evolution at the nanoparticle surfaces
Surface sensitive spectroscopies (e.g., XPS) to probe changes in bonding or defect density as temperature increases
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If nanoparticles on the high-binding-energy support do not exhibit a statistically significant delay in the onset of premelting (or display similar melting behavior to those on the inert support) under identical heating conditions, then the hypothesis that interfacial bonding governs the melting behavior is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: The premelting and melting behavior of high‐entropy alloy nanoparticles is governed by localized lattice strain and heterogeneous bonding at defect sites induced by their atomic-scale compositional disorder. This disorder creates regions with reduced cohesive energy, which serve as nucleation sites for premelting, thereby lowering the effective melting onset temperature compared to conventional (monometallic or low‐entropy) nanoparticles.
drafts.material_initial_state: Nanoparticles synthesized as a single-phase high-entropy alloy (comprising five or more nearly equimolar elements, e.g., Ti, Zr, Hf, Mo, Nb) that are dispersed on inert supports with well-defined sizes (typically <100 nm) and with a crystalline structure exhibiting some surface defects.
drafts.intervention: A controlled heating experiment comparing high-entropy alloy nanoparticles with monometallic or binary nanoparticles of similar size, shape, and support, using identical thermal ramp rates in an inert atmosphere.
drafts.conditions: Ambient pressure in an inert (e.g., argon) atmosphere; temperature ramped gradually from room temperature to a temperature near (but below) the bulk melting points (e.g., up to 0.8–1.0 Tm) to capture the onset of premelting phenomena.
drafts.structural_mediator: Localized atomic-scale lattice distortions and defect sites, especially at nanoparticle surfaces and interfaces, arising from the random distribution of different atomic sizes and bonding preferences inherent to the high configurational entropy.
drafts.mechanism: High configurational entropy leads to a non-uniform distribution of local bond strengths and lattice strains. Defect-rich sites and regions experiencing high atomic misfit possess lower cohesive energies, so atomic mobility and liquid-like disorder emerge at these sites at lower temperatures. This early surface disorder (premelting) then promotes the overall nanoparticle melting process at a depressed temperature relative to more ordered, monometallic nanoparticles.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Under identical thermal conditions, high-entropy alloy nanoparticles will exhibit measurable surface premelting (such as the formation of a thin, disordered or liquid-like layer) at lower temperatures than comparable monometallic/binary nanoparticles. The melting point depression should be more pronounced in HEAs due to their intrinsic lattice heterogeneity.
drafts.baseline: Monometallic or low-entropy binary nanoparticles of similar size, morphology, and support conditions.
drafts.boundary: This hypothesis is expected to hold for nanoparticles up to around 100 nm and for systems where the configurational entropy is high (i.e., those with at least five principal elements). In bulk materials or alloys with minimal atomic size mismatch, the effect may be diminished.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two sets of nanoparticles: one set of high-entropy alloy nanoparticles (e.g., equimolar TiZrHfMoNb) and a baseline set of monometallic or binary nanoparticles of comparable size and morphology, both immobilized on the same type of support. Subject both sets to identical heating protocols in an inert atmosphere while monitoring the structural evolution in situ with high-resolution TEM and performing differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) to detect thermal transitions.
measurements: Onset temperature of surface disorder or premelting via in situ TEM imaging
Exothermic or endothermic peaks in DSC corresponding to phase transitions
X-ray diffraction (XRD) changes confirming structural softening or melting onset
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the high-entropy alloy nanoparticles do not show a statistically significant lower onset temperature for premelting (or measurable melting point depression) compared to the baseline nanoparticles, or if the melting behavior correlates solely with particle size rather than the compositional complexity, then the hypothesis is falsified.
